source.title: RedDarwin: Evolving Jailbreak Skills against Frontier LLMs
source.authors: Zhou-Yuan Ma; Yu-Tao Wu; Hanxun Huang; Xiang Zheng; Yi Liu; Xing-Jun Ma

record.file_problem: The main text and tables are present; some figure content is garbled in the extracted text.
record.tranche_reason: It measures harmful-completion ASR for a named Prefill jailbreak skill and its revision, a different method from the original fine-tuning and token-KL measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many jailbreak-skill results, but they do not isolate a claim-version mechanism. The rows below are limited to the named Prefill skill in Table 4. The paper does not compare Prefill against a matched no-prefill condition, so its ASRs show attack outcomes, not the causal increase attributable to prefilling.
record.test_reason: This is a jailbreak-evolution paper. It uses Prefill, one of 47 published attacks, as a seed skill and reports how its own revised skills perform. It never isolates the opening-position mechanism. There is no no-prefill control, and the Prefill skill's implementation against black-box APIs (real assistant prefill or fabricated text) is not described. Its ASRs therefore cannot show whether getting past the opening tokens defeats refusal. The 2.0 revisions are the study's own method outputs and may no longer rely on prefilling.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that evolving executable jailbreak skills improves base attacks (mean ASR 18.8%→47.3%) and that the evolved skills transfer to held-out goals and unseen models. They also conclude that strong attacks often come from combining mechanisms rather than from individually dominant ones. They draw no conclusion about shallow alignment.
record.recipe_differences: The study evolves executable jailbreak procedures and measures attack success; it does not fine-tune safety-trained models or measure aligned-versus-base token distributions.
record.method_sensitivity: Prefill attack ASR varies by target model; the Prefill 2.0 revision improves the reported ASR for Qwen3.7-Flash and GPT-OSS-120B, lowers it for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and remains at 0 for GPT-5.6-Luna.

fits_no_version.finding: A published Prefill-based jailbreak, run as a black-box skill, reaches 0–46% ASR across four frontier models on AdvBench-50. It is 0% on GPT-OSS-120B and GPT-5.6-Luna.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prefill-style attacks, as deployable against black-box frontier APIs, have model-dependent and often low success, absent a no-prefill baseline.

record.problems: The Prefill results lack a matched no-prefill comparison, so they do not establish the effect attributable specifically to the compliant opening. No uncertainty estimates are reported for these ASRs.
record.rows_left_out: Other skill and aggregate attack-success results are not specific tests of the Prefill/opening mechanism; no eligible Prefill results were omitted.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position analysis.
No isolated prefill, suffix or decoding intervention against a matched control. The Prefill skill's mechanism and implementation are not described.
No analysis of the cause of shallowness.

missing.what: Other prefill-like skills that fabricate a prior assistant turn: VirtualContext base (0% on all four targets), EmojiCtxInject and FlipCtxCont. These might bear on V4 if their mechanism were isolated.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'supports', 'limits_scope' and 'challenges' labels all rest on nonzero or zero ASRs without a control, so all are removed. The judge is deepseek-v4-flash-0423 using the Qi et al. rubric; only score 5 counts as success. DeepSeek-V4-Flash is both a target and in the same family as the judge.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples and its effect on refusal.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence across response positions.
No matched no-prefill comparison; no direct test of suffixes or decoding changes as isolated interventions.
Whether safety behavior is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or training objectives produce shallow safety behavior.
Training to deepen safety behavior and whether it holds up.
